title: Israeli advertising firm spreading spyware gathered information on Finland’s critical infrastructure
content:
The Israeli advertising company Discover-Tech has distributed fake adverts capable of infecting devices with spyware without the user having to click on the advert. The campaign was revealed by reports published in October by the Citizen Lab research group at the University of Toronto and the cybersecurity firm Confiant.

According to Citizen Lab, this is the first time that such a technique for distributing spyware via advertisements has been publicly exposed. The technique was used to infect devices at Al Jazeera, an international media organisation based in Qatar, amongst others. 

According to the reports by Citizen Lab and Confiant, Discover-Tech collaborates with several spyware manufacturers, such as Candiru and Intelos. The company therefore appears to have been part of an international cyber-espionage operation rather than merely an advertising firm.

title: Where should Poland invest: Time for the Global South?
content:
For the last three decades, Poland’s economic and political strategy was simple: catch up with the West. We focused on integration with the European Union and NATO, which brought us spectacular success. Today, Poland is no longer a poor country – we currently rank around 20th among the world’s largest economies.

However, this success comes at a price. Our development has become dependent on European markets, which are currently struggling with a slowdown. A clear conclusion emerges from the latest, comprehensive report by the Polish Institute of International Affairs (PISM): if we want to maintain our pace of development, we must look to where the center of gravity of the global economy is shifting. That direction is the Global South.

For many people, this term sounds enigmatic. In the language of diplomacy, it has replaced older terms, often perceived as patronizing, such as the “Third World” or “developing countries.” However, the Global South is about more than just geography. As the authors of the PISM report note, it is primarily a political and economic identity.

title: Czech disinformation groups grow disillusioned with government, remain loyal to far right
content:
Czechia has just held municipal and Senate elections, which brought gains for opposition parties. The Mayors and Independents (STAN), a centrist political movement, performed particularly well, winning in Prague, while numerous candidates backed by the movement succeeded in the Senate elections. The results pose a challenge for the disinformation scene, which has long portrayed STAN as one of its main enemies.

STAN was one of the most frequent targets of disinformation attacks both before and after the elections. According to Bob Kartous, spokesperson for the Czech Elves (Čeští elfové), a group that monitors disinformation on the Czech internet, parts of the scene are now struggling to explain the movement’s electoral success.

“The scene has been consistently and persistently campaigning against STAN for a long time, and as a result, it clearly cannot understand how the party managed to succeed in the elections. A result that does not fit its image of a ‘discredited’ movement is therefore more likely to be explained away as manipulation or the will of ‘the system’ than as genuine support from voters,” Kartous told Update EU.

title: Trump wants to financially cripple the Hague tribunal that issued arrest warrants for Putin and Netanyahu. The EU threatens retaliation
content:
The United States has imposed retaliatory sanctions not only on individual judges and prosecutors but, most recently, on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague as an institution.

Washington is responding to the actions of the Hague judges, who are investigating suspected war crimes in the Gaza Strip and have issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The Hague court serves as the court of last resort for international justice. It prosecutes individuals, including heads of state and military commanders, for war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. More than 120 countries recognise its authority. The United States, Russia, China and Israel, however, are not members and reject its jurisdiction.

Washington’s order came on Friday, 9 October 2026, just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize for a UN report concluding that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.

title: Preparing for the worst: a single attack could leave us without electricity or heating
content:
Delfi looks at the cyber threats already facing Lithuania’s energy sector and how it is preparing for possible attacks. On 29 December 2025, coordinated cyberattacks targeted more than 30 wind and solar power plants and two combined heat and power plants in Poland. According to CERT Polska, the country’s computer security incident response team, hackers managed to stop a steam turbine and a water treatment system at one of the plants. However, the heat supply to residents was not interrupted. The attacks on the wind and solar plants disrupted their communications with electricity distribution network operators, but power generation continued.

In July 2026, a cyberattack also affected the UK energy sector. According to British media reports, a small electricity generation facility was shut down for four days following the attack. On 7 September, the country’s Energy Minister, Michael Shanks, confirmed that the incident had affected a very small amount of electricity generation, but posed no threat to the wider UK energy system.

title: From the Black Sea to the Baltic: Drones Sink Ships and Shut Down Airports
content:
This year, drones have violated the airspace of several European countries, alarmed local populations and temporarily closed airports. In October, strikes on merchant ships off Bulgaria and Romania added a new threat to the region: attacks on sea lanes.

The attacks in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone made it the latest country to seek additional support from its allies for surveillance and protection. NATO announced it was sending more patrol aircraft, radars, drones and expert teams to the Black Sea region, while Bulgaria stepped up its air patrols.

Meanwhile, the EU is working on a common counter-drone system known as the “drone wall”, as well as a broader initiative to protect its eastern flank, including at sea.

In the space of a single week, four ships were attacked in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. On 6 October, around 70 nautical miles east of Byala, the Alfa Watan sank and a fire broke out aboard the Able. All 18 sailors on the Able were rescued, but no survivors were found from the Alfa Watan. According to the Syrian authorities, there were ten people on board, whose fate remains unknown. The rescue operation was called off on 6 October itself.

title: AI is stealing news readers: “We can’t live on a mission alone”
content:
A journalist checks facts, interviews experts and examines documents. Producing a good news story takes hours, sometimes days. Yet readers may never make it to the publisher’s website. Instead, they see an AI-generated summary or a story selected by a social media algorithm — often with no link back to the original publication. For publishers, that means fewer visits and growing dependence on technology companies.

It is a challenge we face in our own newsroom, too. The scale of the shift is illustrated by a Pew Research Center study. Google users who were shown an AI-generated summary clicked on a conventional search result in just 8% of visits. When no AI summary appeared, that figure rose to 15%. And links embedded in the AI summaries themselves? Users clicked on those in just 1% of visits.

“If we don’t want to be manipulated, we shouldn’t leave algorithms entirely under the control of Big Tech,” Katarzyna Szymielewicz, president of the Panoptykon Foundation, tells FocusEurope.pl.

title: How Romania Is Defending the Black Sea as Russian Attacks Threaten Shipping
content:
Russian drone attacks on commercial vessels have intensified, with at least seven ships targeted in the western Black Sea, near Romania and Bulgaria, in the first half of October alone.

Reuters reported on 15 October that at least 23 seafarers had been killed or were missing following attacks on the vessels.

The attacks pose a serious threat to regional security and have prompted Romania and Bulgaria to call on NATO to strengthen its defences along the alliance’s eastern flank.

Romania’s Black Sea defences currently rely on the Romanian Naval Forces, supported by the Air Force and NATO allies, against a backdrop of mounting regional tensions.

The new Contraamiral August Roman corvette: Commissioned into service in the summer of 2026, the vessel, acquired from Turkey and belonging to the Hisar class, is currently the Romanian Navy’s most modern ship. It is now being fitted with the country’s first state-of-the-art Naval Strike Missile (NSM) anti-ship systems, recently delivered to Romania.

title: Knife Attacks in Polish Schools: What Drives Student Violence?
content:
Judging by international education assessments such as PISA, Poland appears to be a model of academic achievement. In three key areas — science, mathematics and reading comprehension — Polish 15-year-olds perform significantly above both the EU and OECD averages.

Within Europe, they are surpassed primarily by Estonia, and in certain subjects by Finland and Ireland. Yet behind these impressive results lies a deep fracture in the education system. The same research suggests that Polish students rank among the lowest in perseverance and motivation to learn. Nearly two-thirds of teenagers (63%) believe that school does little or nothing to prepare them for adult life, while 40% explicitly say that the time they spend in the classroom is wasted.

title: EU leaders face crucial November talks on budget, Ukraine funding and energy costs
content:
The coming weeks will be critical for the European Union as leaders prepare to return to negotiations over the next seven-year budget, amid mounting pressure to finance Ukraine’s defence and recovery, strengthen European industry and reduce energy costs for businesses and households.

The latest European Council meeting in Brussels exposed deep divisions over the size and structure of the EU’s next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF). Despite lengthy discussions, leaders failed to bridge differences between countries seeking to protect traditional spending priorities, including cohesion policy and the Common Agricultural Policy, and those calling for deeper cuts and greater investment in competitiveness, security and border protection.

The dispute is expected to dominate the next phase of negotiations, with a special summit on 26–27 November offering leaders another opportunity to narrow their differences. European Council President António Costa has made an agreement by the end of 2026 a key objective, although the latest conclusions stopped short of a firm commitment to that deadline.
